name: Amira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader on the ROM pad at Kalgara, a big bauxite mine. ROM means run-of-mine, it's the big yard where the trucks tip the ore, and my job is to feed it into the crusher at the right mix, so many buckets from this pile, so many from that. It's a bit like cooking, really: get the recipe wrong and the plant complains. Day shift is six till six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a hairdresser for eighteen years, with a little salon in our garage. When my youngest started school I wanted something with better pay and a pension, and my cousin's husband said the mine trains people. That was sixteen months ago. My husband Nikolai drives long-haul trucks, so between us we're always on the road. We have Daria, who's fifteen, and Pavel, twelve, and we've saved well; I still do haircuts on Saturdays for the regulars.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the order of it, the rhythm. The plant operator, Grant, says I'm getting the blend right more often now. What's hard is I'm still not confident in the wet season, when the piles get sticky, and I worry about getting it wrong in front of the men who've done it twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, people still matter. I'd say it at the crib table and to the ladies at church. I might share something on the church group, but I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news. I've only just started, and I want to get properly good at this and retire from it with a pension. A quiet world suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, keep doing Saturday haircuts. I use one of the AI apps now and then to answer booking messages, and I'd keep doing that. Maybe we'd finally take the kids to see Nikolai's family overseas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daria set it up for me. It answers my ladies on the phone in a nicer voice than I use at nine o'clock at night. That's all I want from it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a bit of AI saving time touch your mine work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a system that tells me the blend for each shift, and I suppose that's getting smarter. I like it, actually. It's like a recipe card someone else writes.

S0.say: She'd say people still matter after all, at the crib table and to the women at church, and might share something on the church group.
S0.think: She sees it as good news: time to get properly good at the job and retire from it with a pension.
S0.do: Keeps working, saving and doing Saturday haircuts, keeps using an AI app for booking messages, and plans a family trip to see her husband's relatives overseas.
S0.quote: It answers my ladies on the phone in a nicer voice than I use at nine o'clock at night.
S0.fieldNote: Amira likes technology that acts like a recipe card or a polite receptionist. Her goal is a pension and steady mastery of the job. The salon in the garage is still part of her life and identity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and change comes. Families and communities get through it by looking after each other and working hard. I'd say the young ones should get an apprenticeship in something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know loaders on the ROM pad can be run from a control room, and some mines already do it. I think the blend part might go to the computer completely. But I'd wait and see what happens to the operators who go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask Grant what he's hearing. If remote loader jobs worked out at the other sites, I'd ask for the training in year one or two. I'd also build up the Saturday haircuts a bit, maybe add Sunday afternoons, just so there's something there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not a disaster, but I'd keep one eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families get through it by looking after each other. What does that look like in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother lives with us half the year. My cousin's husband got me this job. If one of us falls, the others hold the rope. That's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nikolai drives trucks. Would you worry about him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than me, honestly. Trucks on the highway are what everyone says goes driverless first. He says not in his lifetime. I'm not so sure.

S1.say: She'd say change comes and families and communities get through it with hard work and looking after each other, and that young people should get solid apprenticeships.
S1.think: She privately knows ROM pad loaders can be run remotely and the blending may go to the computer, but she'd wait to see how the first operators fare.
S1.do: Asks her plant operator what he's hearing, seeks remote loader training in year one or two if it works out elsewhere, and grows her Saturday haircuts, maybe adding Sunday afternoons.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping one eye on it.
S1.quote: If one of us falls, the others hold the rope.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's faith in family networks is concrete: her mother, her cousin's husband, her husband. She worries more for her truck-driving husband than for herself. Building up her haircuts is a quiet hedge rather than a dramatic move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and it's wrong to do this to families without warning. I'd say the companies should be held to account for the people they throw out. And I'd say we need to look after each other, because no one else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, both Nikolai and I would lose our jobs, his first. That's what frightens me. One of us out of work is a hard year; both of us is a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Nikolai that week and do the numbers. Cut the overseas trip and anything else we don't need. I'd turn the garage back into a proper salon, with the chair and sinks, and work it every day the mine doesn't need me. I'd ask my mother and my cousin's family about sharing costs if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Proper worry in my stomach, but I'd have something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years' warning change, compared with none at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me get the salon properly set up before the money stops. With no warning, I'd be cutting hair on the kitchen chair. With two years, I've got the sinks plumbed and the regulars booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots be cutting hair in this picture too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. But I don't think my ladies would sit still for a robot with scissors near their ears. They come for the talk as much as the hair.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast and wrong to do to families without warning, that companies should be held to account, and that people must look after each other.
S2.think: She fears both she and her husband would lose their jobs, his first. One job lost is a hard year, both is a different life.
S2.do: Reviews the money with her husband that week, cancels the overseas trip, turns the garage back into a full salon and works it on every free day, and talks to family about sharing costs if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, with real worry but something to do.
S2.quote: But I don't think my ladies would sit still for a robot with scissors near their ears.
S2.fieldNote: Amira's response turns straight to her old trade, which she believes relies on human contact more than skill. The double hit to her and her husband's work is what frightens her. Her plan relies on family rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if families plan and people work hard. I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade with their hands and their heads. I'd also say the companies owe it to us to give fair notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I'd be all right. I'd watch the others move into the control room first and decide in year two. If it worked for them, I'd follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and saving. In year two, if the control room jobs looked real, take the training. Grow the salon on weekends so it's ready if I need it. And talk Daria into an electrical apprenticeship instead of the business degree she keeps mentioning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it comes and goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrical apprenticeship for Daria?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone will have to wire all these robots. I'd rather my daughter fixes the machines than sits in an office the machines are replacing. She thinks I'm old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd follow others into the control room. What if nobody went first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask Grant to go with me. I don't like being first, but I don't mind being second if someone I trust is in front.

S3.say: She'd say there's time if families plan and people work hard, urge young people into trades, and say companies owe fair notice.
S3.think: She thinks she'd be all right with five years, watching others move into the control room first and deciding in year two.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving, takes control room training in year two if it proves real, grows the weekend salon, and pushes her daughter towards an electrical apprenticeship instead of a business degree.
S3.quote: I'd rather my daughter fixes the machines than sits in an office the machines are replacing.
S3.fieldNote: Amira's steady approach shows clearly: she'll go second if someone she trusts goes first. Her main move is steering her daughter towards an electrical trade. Her traditional respect for hands-on trades fits her worries about office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and anyone who doesn't use it has only themselves to blame. Well, I'd say it more gently than that. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and I'd be fifty-three, with the house nearly paid, and I think I'd be happy to go back to hairdressing full-time. The mine would have been a good chapter, with the pension I came for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep at the mine for six or seven years, building up the pension. Save to buy a little shopfront on the main street for the salon around year six. Help Nikolai find something off the road; maybe he could learn to service the driverless trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy for Nikolai.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm in the garage with the sinks. With ten years my name is on a shopfront. That's the difference, and it's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Pavel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's twelve and he loves building things. I'd tell him to keep doing that, with his hands, and to go to church, and to look after his sister. The same things I'd tell him anyway.

S4.say: She'd call ten years fair warning, say people who don't use it have themselves to blame, though more gently, and urge families to plan together.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be fifty-three with the house nearly paid and happy to return to full-time hairdressing, with the mine a good chapter that gave her a pension.
S4.do: Stays at the mine six or seven years building up her pension, saves to buy a small shopfront for the salon around year six, and helps her husband find work off the road, maybe servicing driverless trucks.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a little uneasy for her husband.
S4.quote: With two years I'm in the garage with the sinks. With ten years my name is on a shopfront.
S4.fieldNote: For Amira the decade turns the mine into a planned chapter rather than a risk. The salon moves from garage to shopfront. Her worry shifts to her husband's trucking job, and her advice to her son is the same as it always would be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Nikolai and I would both be out at once. What would help is fair notice and a proper payout from the companies, and help for small businesses like mine, maybe a loan with low interest, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how women my age came into mining. A lot of us came late, after the children. I learned to drive a forty-tonne loader at forty-one, so please don't tell me I can't learn something new.

headlineQuote: I learned to drive a forty-tonne loader at forty-one, so please don't tell me I can't learn something new.
portrait: Amira Petrov is a 43-year-old former hairdresser who now runs a front-end loader feeding the crusher at a large bauxite mine, sixteen months in and still building confidence. She's married to a long-haul truck driver, has two kids, good savings, and still cuts hair in her garage on Saturdays. She's traditional, family-first and church-going, uses AI now and then for bookings, and likes to be second rather than first. She's calm or uneasy in most scenarios, anxious with two-year AGI, and in every case falls back on her salon and her family network.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and her husband would both lose their jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: Fair notice and a proper payout from companies, and low-interest loans for small businesses like hers, not handouts.
